clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant tumour-predisposition syndrome caused by inactivating variants in CDC73 (formerly HRPT2), encoding parafibromin
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the dominant feature and is unusual for its high rate of parathyroid carcinoma or atypical adenoma
The syndrome links parathyroid disease with ossifying fibromas of the mandible and maxilla, which are distinct from the brown tumours of hyperparathyroidism
Renal manifestations include cysts, hamartomas, and Wilms-like tumours, and uterine tumours occur in women
Compared with other familial hyperparathyroidism, the hypercalcaemia is often severe and single-gland disease with malignant potential is characteristic
Management is surgical for the parathyroid disease with a low threshold to consider carcinoma, alongside surveillance for jaw, renal, and uterine lesions
Consider HPT-JT in young or severe primary hyperparathyroidism, especially with a jaw lesion or family history, and test CDC73
reference.pathophysiology: CDC73 encodes parafibromin, a component of the PAF1 transcriptional regulatory complex that acts as a tumour suppressor influencing gene expression and cell proliferation. Germline inactivating variants, combined with a somatic second hit in target tissues, remove this suppressor function and predispose to tumour formation. In the parathyroid glands this produces adenomas, atypical adenomas, and an elevated risk of carcinoma, with resulting primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcaemia. Loss of parafibromin in bone of the jaw gives rise to ossifying fibromas, and its loss in the kidney and uterus underlies the cystic, hamartomatous, and neoplastic lesions at those sites. The malignant potential in the parathyroid distinguishes this syndrome from other inherited forms of hyperparathyroidism.
additionalDifferentials: Parathyroid carcinoma without a recognised syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone confirming primary hyperparathyroidism
Parathyroid imaging (ultrasound and sestamibi) to localise disease
Orthopantomogram or jaw imaging for ossifying fibromas
Renal imaging for cysts, hamartomas, and tumours
Pelvic imaging for uterine tumours in women
CDC73 gene sequencing and testing of at-risk relatives
redFlags: Very high serum calcium with a palpable neck mass suggesting parathyroid carcinoma
Haematuria or a renal mass suggesting a Wilms-like tumour
Recurrent or persistent hyperparathyroidism after surgery indicating malignancy
reference.prognosis: The prognosis depends chiefly on whether parathyroid carcinoma develops, since malignant disease can recur and metastasise; benign hyperparathyroidism and jaw and renal lesions are manageable with surgery and surveillance, and early recognition improves outcomes.
pitfalls: Treating severe hyperparathyroidism as benign and missing a parathyroid carcinoma
Mistaking a jaw ossifying fibroma for a brown tumour of hyperparathyroidism
Failing to offer genetic testing and family screening in young or severe cases
Omitting renal and uterine surveillance once the syndrome is confirmed
references: OMIM entry for hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome
management: Parathyroidectomy is the definitive treatment; perform en bloc resection with wide margins and avoid capsular rupture whenever parathyroid carcinoma or an atypical adenoma is suspected
Medically control hypercalcaemia when surgery is deferred or in unresectable carcinoma using a calcimimetic (cinacalcet), with a bisphosphonate for skeletal protection
Treat acute hypercalcaemic crisis with intravenous saline rehydration, a loop diuretic once volume-replete, and a bisphosphonate or calcimimetic
Undertake lifelong surveillance for extra-parathyroid lesions with periodic jaw imaging for ossifying fibromas, renal imaging for cysts and hamartomas, and pelvic imaging for uterine tumours in women
Monitor serum calcium and parathyroid hormone after surgery for persistent or recurrent disease, given the malignant potential of the parathyroid tumours
Offer genetic counselling with CDC73 testing of the patient and cascade screening of at-risk relatives
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across endocrine surgery, endocrinology, clinical genetics, oncology and oral-maxillofacial surgery
